Borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Latin vallum. Alternatively from Proto-Indo-European *wel- (“to turn, wind, roll”).

Alternatively from Proto-Albanian *(e)reug-, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁rewg- (“to retch, vomit”). Cognate to Ancient Greek ἐρεύγομαι (ereúgomai, “to belch, gurk”).

Borrowed from Vulgar Latin *aeramem m, whence also Italian rame, from Latin aeramen n. The variant ram reflects the variant Vulgar Latin *aeramum m, whence also Sicilian ramu, Venetan ramo, while Tosk rëm can reflect either forms.

From Proto-Albanian *rāšja, from *(H)rōs-ye/o-, apparently a denominative of either Proto-Indo-European *h₁rṓs (from *h₁ers- (“to flow; moisture, dew”); compare Latin rōs (“dew”)) or a different root noun *h₁róh₁s (from *h₁reh₁s- (“to run, rush”); compare Old English rǣs (“running, race”), Latin rōr

From Proto-Albanian *(h)eríja- 'of this time, from this time, presently, of now > new, recent', a derivative of Alb. herë '(one) time, hour' etc., which is an old loan-word from Latin hōra 'time, hour' etc.; the Albanian substantive is historically not compatible with a reconstruction Proto-Indo-Eur

From Proto-Albanian *wragtja, related to rrah. Alternatively from Proto-Albanian *raT(ś)i-, from Proto-Indo-European *ureh1ǵ(h)- (“to strike, beat”). Cognate to Ancient Greek ῥάττω (rháttō, “to strike, beat”).

A term with multiple plausible etymologies. Either from Latin rāpum (“turnip”), Ancient Greek ῥάπυς (rhápus, “turnip”), or Proto-Slavic *rěpa (“turnip, beet”), or natively from Proto-Indo-European *(s)rā́ps. First attested as rrap, producing the contemporary form through plural metaphony and the Arb

From Proto-Albanian *rina, from Proto-Indo-European *h₃er- (“to move, stir”), compare Ancient Greek ὄρνυμι (órnumi, “to raise; arouse; stir up”), Sanskrit ऋणोति (ṛṇóti, “to rise, move”). From Proto-Albanian *wrīpa. Compare Ancient Greek ῥάπτω (rháptō, “to sew together, to stitch”), Lithuanian verpti (“to spin”). Alternatively from Proto-Albanian *reipa, to be connected with Proto-Germanic *raipaz (“rope”), in Old High German reif (“rope, cord”), Middle Low German rēp (“sling, rope”)

From Proto-Albanian *writja, from Proto-Indo-European *wert- (“to turn”); cognate with Sanskrit वर्तते (vartate), Latin vertere, German werden (“to become”). Alternatively, a derivative of rri. According to Matasović, the etymology is controversial and has no accepted source or substrate

parole.significato: to watch over, to observe, to guard
parole.testo: From Proto-Albanian *rāgnja, connected to Old Norse røkja (“to take care of”), Greek ἀρήγω (arígo, “to assist, to defend”). Alternatively from Proto-Albanian *(a)ru(u)ē-, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂rew- (“to get light, brighten”). Compare Armenian արև (arew, “sun”).

parole.significato: Ragusa (former name of Dubrovnik: a port city in southern Croatia, on the Adriatic Sea)
parole.testo: From Proto-Albanian *rāguša Compare Sicilian Ragusa. Alternatively from Latin Ragusium. Regarded as a quite early loanword as the /ɡ/ is dropped, a pattern in older loanwords such as mjeshtër from magister, Drisht from Drivastum, mjek from medicus, and pyll from palūs, palūdem.

From Proto-Albanian *si-a, a combination of two pronominal members, Proto-Indo-European *kʷih₂ and *h₂ew-/*h₂en-. Alternatively from Proto-Albanian *tšja or, as per Meyer, from Greek σαν (san, “when, whenever”).

Çabej derives it, together with cakorre and cakicë, from cak, a lexicalization of the onomatopoeic theme, resembling the sound of a cut. Alternatively, from a South Slavic language, compare Serbo-Croatian sekira, Macedonian секавица (sekavica), Bulgarian сакавица (sakavica), though they have given s
Borrowed from Latin secundus directly or from Italian secondo.

From Proto-Albanian *tsjam tam, from Proto-Indo-European *kiom tom, a sequence of two pronouns in neuter of which the first is related to 'se'. Alternatively from Proto-Albanian *tśe enta, literally 'this being', the first element from *kwe- (“how, what”), or *k̂(e) (“this”), while the second one be

parole.significato: female gown (made of wool, covering the shoulders and the chest)
parole.testo: Either from Proto-Germanic *sarkiz (“shirt, armour, hauberk”), via Gothic or from Proto-Slavic *sorka (“shirt”). Schuhard and Meyer claim a borrowing from either Latin serica or Latin sarica.

Compare Hittite [Term?] (/⁠šarra⁠/, “break, rupture, divide”), Latin serra (“id”), Lithuanian sėris (“filament”). Alternatively borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Latin serra; compare Aromanian sharã.

Unclear. Either from the same root as Ancient Greek σκορπίος (skorpíos), Proto-Indo-European *(s)ker-, or from shkrep, since scorpions are usually found on rocks. Alternatively a borrowing from Latin scorpiō.

From Proto-Albanian *iš-kruma, with a non etymological -mb-<*m (cf. According to Guillaume Bonnet, possibly from Proto-Germanic *skurtaz. Alternatively borrowed from reconstructed Vulgar Latin *excurtus (cf. From shkurt + -oj; hence shkurtoj (“to cut; make short”). Alternatively borrowed from Late Latin excurtō, from Latin curtō; cf. Romanian scurta, Aromanian shcurtedz.

Either from a tabooistic description derived from lig, or from *lligë, from Proto-Albanian *sligā, the same Indo-European root of Old Irish selige (“turtle”) and German schleichen (“to crawl”), from Proto-Indo-European *sleyg-, *sleyǵ- (“to glide, smooth, spread”).

Enlargement with the collective suffix -dh(ë) of variant shparr. Alternatively from Proto-Albanian *is-pardza, from Proto-Indo-European *perǵ- (compare Lithuanian pérgas (“fishing canoe”), Polish próg (“threshold, doorstep”)).

From Proto-Albanian *sparna, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *speh₁- (or possibly Proto-Indo-European *sper-). Compare Old English spær (“sparing, scant”), Latin (pro)sperus (“lucky”), Old Church Slavonic споръ (sporŭ, “plentiful”), Ancient Greek σπαρνός (sparnós, “rare”), Sanskrit स्फिर (sphirá

From Proto-Albanian * ̊peri-, from Proto-Indo-European *per- (“to bear, lead across, penetrate”). Cognate to Ancient Greek πείρω (peírō, “to get through, pierce”). Alternatively reconstructed as from Proto-Albanian *eś-per-, from PIE *eǵʰs- (“out”) + *pi-pér- (“to bring out”).
Either from Proto-Indo-European *per- (“to bear, lead across, penetrate”) (cf. shpoj and shporr), or a loanword from Gothic, through an unattested Vulgar Latin *spora.
Either a prefixal derivative of laj or borrowed from Vulgar Latin *experlavāre, from Late Latin perlavāre, from Latin lavō. Compare Romanian spăla, Aromanian aspel.

From sh- + për- + thyej, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱeh₃i- (“to sharpen”). Alternatively from Proto-Indo-European *sperǵʰ- (“to spring, jump”). Compare Lithuanian spreñgti (“to push in”), Old Church Slavonic прѧсти (pręsti, “to spin, stretch”), Ancient Greek σπέρχω (spérkhō, “to hasten”), Sanskrit स्

From Vulgar Latin *expedītāre, from Latin expedīre (“to entrict, disengage”). Alternatively, a verbal formation with a prefix denoting the movement away from something from Proto-Indo-European *peth₂- (“to spread out; to fly”), connected to pjetë (“upwards”).

From either Proto-Albanian *śe(p)tá-tā, or Proto-Albanian *źe(p)tá-tā, from Proto-Indo-European *septḿ̥-t-, a suffixed form originally meaning "group of seven", from Proto-Indo-European *septḿ̥. From Old Albanian shtanse, from *shtan + -zë, from Proto-Albanian *stana, from Proto-Indo-European *sth₂-nó-s (“standing”), participle of *steh₂- (“to stand”). Ultimately a doublet of stër-. Alternatively, from Dacian or Paleo-Balkan substrate, cognate to Romanian stână.

From either Proto-Albanian *sternā, from Proto-Indo-European *ster-neh₂, or Proto-Albanian *sterjā, from Proto-Indo-European *stér-ih₂ ~ *str̥-yéh₂-s, both from Proto-Indo-European *ster- (“barren”). Alternatively borrowed from Romanian știră (“sterile”).

From Proto-Albanian *štramba, close to Old Prussian strambo (“stubble”), Lithuanian strampas (“club, truncheon”), and Proto-Germanic *strambaz, in Norwegian dial, stramb (“strong smell”), Middle Low German stram (“strong, powerful”). Alternatively a derivative of Vulgar Latin *strambus, from Latin s

Singularized plural of *shtër-ez, based on *shtërë, from shtroj (cf. shtredhë). Alternatively from Proto-Albanian *steura, from Proto-Germanic *steuro (“steering paddle, rudder, stern”), from *steurjan (“to steer”) (cf. Old English stéor).

From Proto-Albanian *stūlā- or *stūlwā-, from Proto-Indo-European *stuh₂-l-eh₂ < *steh₂- (“to stand up”). Compare Ancient Greek στῦλος (stûlos), Proto-Slavic *stъlbъ (“post, pillar”). Alternatively from Byzantine Greek στῦλος (stûlos) or from Latin stilus (“stake, spike”) .

From Proto-Albanian *štanga, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *st(h₂)eug-, from *steyh₂-. Compare Sanskrit स्त्यायते (styāyate, “it hardens”), Ancient Greek στῖον (stîon, “pebble”), Russian стена́ (stená, “wall”), Old English stān (“stone”). Alternatively cognate to Old Norse stinga (“to put, to

Ultimately from Hungarian szoba (“stove”), either through Ottoman Turkish صوبا (soba, “stove”) or Serbo-Croatian sȍba /со̏ба (“room; (archaic) stove”), possibly even a conflation of both sources. Doublet of stufë.
Either an onomatopoeia, related to cek, or related to Vulgar Latin *toccare, itself from Frankish *tukkōn (“to touch, hit”), with continuants in Italian toccare, French toucher (“to touch”).

Uncertain. According to Çabej, the word is attested in Pult. It could be an early borrowing from Doric Greek θωράκειον (thōrákeion) or θωράκιον (thōrákion), a diminutive of θώραξ (thṓrax, “breastplate, cuirass, corselet”), or directly from the latter. parole.significato: to toast, brown, warm one's feet
parole.testo: From Proto-Albanian *ϑeuk-, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱewk- (“to glow, burn, lighten”). Perhaps related to flak (“flame”). Cognates include Avestan 𐬯𐬀𐬊𐬐 (saok), Northern Kurdish sotin and Persian سوختن (suxtan, “to burn”). Also compare Ancient Greek τήκω (tḗkō, “melt, dissolve”) Alternatively relate

parole.significato: scrap of cloth (used for repairing or stuffing clothes or mattresses)
parole.testo: From thelë + -më. Alternatively from a hypothetical Proto-Indo-European *ḱelmn̥, enlargement of Proto-Indo-European *ḱel- (“to cover; hide; protect”) (cf. kallëm), a formation paralleling Latin tegimen which also used a Proto-Indo-European root meaning 'to cover'.

From Proto-Albanian *tˢ́ika, from Pre-Proto-Albanian *ćīkā ~ *ćeykā, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱeh₃- (“to sharpen”). A PPA form *ćīkā supports a Proto-Indo-European *k̑iH-keh2- form, while *ćeykā supports a Proto-Indo-European *k̑éi̯H-keh2- form. The absence of an a-umlaut favors against a short -i-

parole.significato: to contract, draw together, shrink up
parole.testo: Denominative verb from *kurr and prefix të-, from Proto-Albanian *kurna, whence kurriz; see there for more. Alternatively, from Proto-Albanian *kurn-, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)ker- (“to bend, curve, turn”). Cognate to Ancient Greek κυρτός (kurtós, “crooked, bent”) and Latin curvus (“bent, curved

parole.significato: to pull (a boat to the coast)
parole.testo: Uncertain; possibly from Proto-Albanian *tratja, from *tra + *-atja, from Proto-Indo-European *tr̥h₂-é-ti, from *terh₂- (“to cross over, pass through”). Alternatively borrowed from Romanian tras (“pulled”), past participle of trage (“to pull”).

From Proto-Albanian *trim-, most likely from Proto-Indo-European *ter- (“soft, weak, young”). Cognate with Sanskrit तरुण (táruṇa, “young”) and Armenian թարմ (tʻarm, “young, fresh”). Alternatively from Proto-Indo-European *trem(s)- (“to thump; to tremble”). Compare Latin tremō (“tremble”), Lithuanian

Likely from Proto-Albanian *wadza, from Proto-Indo-European *woǵʰ-eh₂, from *weǵʰ- (“to bring, carry”), cognate with Proto-Germanic *wegaz (“way, path”). Alternatively: * from Proto-Albanian *wada with unexpected aspiration, from Proto-Indo-European *wodʰ-eh₂, from *wedʰ- (“to lead; to bring”) or *w

From Proto-Albanian *warā, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂wer- (“to cover”) (compare Messapic urios (“doors”), Oscan veru (“door”), Old Norse vǫr (“row of stones”), ver (“dam”)). Either from Proto-Albanian *wa(d), from Proto-Indo-European *weh₂dʰ- (“to go, walk”), or from Latin vadum; impossible to determine. Possibly forms a doublet of vete.

parole.significato: fold, pen, cote (fenced area, in which the small cattle is herded together for the night)
parole.testo: From Proto-Albanian *au̯aϑā, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂wes- (“to dwell, abide, pass/stay the night”). Cognate to Sanskrit वास (vāsá-, “sojourn, stay, spending the night”), प्रौष्ठ (próṣṭha-, “lodging”). Alternatively from an unattested *vartë, from Proto-Albanian *wartā, close to Tocharian B wärto

From Proto-Albanian *awa-derna (“to go away”), from Proto-Indo-European *drem- (“to run”). Cognate to (aorist) Ancient Greek ἔδραμον (édramon, “to run away”), Sanskrit द्राति (drāti, “to run, to hasten”). Alternatively from v- + djerr.

From Proto-Albanian *wīdza, from Proto-Indo-European *winǵos (compare Lithuanian vi̇̀nkšna, Polish wiąz), variant of *wiǵo (compare English wych elm, Northern Kurdish bizî). Alternatively from Proto-Indo-European *widʰu-, in which case it could be linked with Old Dutch widu, Old Norse viðr (Danish a

From Proto-Albanian *awa-rapa, derivative of *repa (“to strip off, tear off”) (modern rrjep). For sense development, compare Ancient Greek ἔδρᾱν (édrān, “ran away”), from δέρω (dérō, “skin, flay”). More at rrjep. Alternatively from Proto-Indo-European *werb- (“to turn, wind”). Compare Ancient Greek

* From dialectal Italian vrica, derived from Ancient Greek μυρίκη (muríkē). * Alternatively derived from verr.

From Proto-Albanian *awa-rula, possibly related to Latin rotulare (“to roll, revolve”). Compare Middle English rollen, Old French roler. Alternatively from Proto-Albanian *awa-rāgula, close to Proto-Slavic *krǫgъ (“circle”). Related to vrangull.

A methatesized formation from an earlier *vëndër, from Proto-Albanian *ŭ(n)dərā, from Proto-Indo-European *wedʰrom. Compare Old Church Slavonic ведро (vedro, “fine weather”), Old Norse veðr (“wind, air, weather”), Old English weder. Alternatively from Proto-Albanian *awa-raunta, a derivative of rënd

From Proto-Albanian *awena, an innovation based on *au̯e (“down, off”) (cf. Sanskrit अव (áva, “id”)), replacing Proto-Indo-European *dʰeh₁- (“to place, put”). The original meaning must have been 'to put down, put aside', as in Latin pōnere (“to put”). Alternatively from Proto-Albanian *u̯enō, from P
Kristoforidhi and Çabej descend it from South Slavic. Alternatively from Turkish vidalı (“threaded, screwed”).

From Old Albanian ȳll (/yːɫ/), from Proto-Albanian *usla, from either * Proto-Indo-European *h₁us-los (“the burning one”) (compare Old English ysle (“hot ashes”)), from *h₁ews- (“to burn”) (compare Latin ūrere, Ancient Greek εὕω (heúō, “to singe”)); or * from Proto-Indo-European *h₂us-los (“the glow
Possibly from Latin iānua (“door, entrance”), prefixed with z-. Alternatively related to gëloj (“to burst out”). Çabej analyses a possible older form of Proto-Albanian *glon-.

A prefixed formation based on Proto-Albanian *gripa, cognate to Old High German krapfo (“hook”) and Old Norse krappr (“narrow”). Alternatively from Proto-Indo-European *grep- (“hook”), from *gremb- (“crooked, uneven”), from *ger- (“to turn, bend, twist”), same root as grep (“hook”).

parole.significato: to immerse, dunk, sink, to dip
parole.testo: From Proto-Albanian *diš-ūd-tja, a similar formation to mbys, from Proto-Indo-European *wed- (“water”). Alternatively, to be compared with Lithuanian žū́ti (“perish”), žudýti (“slay”), Latvian zùdu (“disappear, get lost”), zaudêt (“lose”), Middle Irish gúas (“danger, peril, jeopardy”).

From Proto-Albanian *džārnā with long *ā < *ē, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷerh₃- (“to swallow”). Close to Lithuanian žarnà (“gut”), Latvian zarna (“intestines”), Old Norse gǫrn (“gut”). Alternatively from *ǵʰer- (“guts, entrails, bowels, intestine”).
* From Proto-Albanian *dis-warka, derivative of *wera (modern vjerr, var) + diminutive -ka. * Alternatively borrowed from Gothic *swairhs.
Possibly from Latin usūra. Alternatively borrowed from Ottoman Turkish [script needed] (yzër).
From Proto-Albanian *tšapā, possibly from Proto-Indo-European *kop- (“to dig”). Cognate with Russian копы́то (kopýto, “to dig”). Alternatively, an alternative form of capë (“claw mattock”).

From Proto-Albanian *anj, close to Sanskrit अनीति (ániti, “blow out”), Gothic 𐌿𐌶𐌰𐌽𐌰𐌽 (uzanan, “blow out”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂enh₁- (“to breathe”). Alternatively from Proto-Albanian *aidn(i)-, from Proto-Indo-European *Hoid- (“to swell”). Cognate to Old Armenian այտնում (aytnum, “to swell”)
